To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a new physiologically-based model of insulin extraction after a meal has been developed and tested.

a three-compartment model for insulin kinetics and an index of hepatic insulin clearance depending on plasma glucose concentration, provide an improved description of glucose regulation in normal subjects.

a new physiologically-based model for the quantitative description of hepatic insulin removal after a meal was developed, and that this model allows a better understanding of glucose metabolism in humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of mathematical models that are able to quantitatively describe the regulation of carbohydrate homeostasis, with the ultimate goal of providing tools for a better management of diabetes.
the development of a model for the description of glucose and insulin kinetics in normal subjects, after a meal, with the aim of providing a quantitative estimate of TIE.
the development of a model that allows a better description of the glucose metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model developed here provides a better understanding of the regulation of glucose metabolism, and is useful for the assessment of the effects of drugs and/or disease states on glucose metabolism.
the proposed model is a useful tool for the assessment of insulin kinetics, and in particular for the estimation of TIE after a meal.
the new TIE model allows the estimation of the basal and total TIE, and the sensitivity of TIE to glucose.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a model that can be used to estimate TIE, which is a key parameter for the regulation of carbohydrate homeostasis.
the new model allows the quantitative estimation of hepatic insulin clearance after a meal, thus providing a useful tool in the study of glucose regulation.

the three-compartment model, coupled with TIF depending on glucose concentration showed the best fit, the good ability to precisely estimates the parameters, and provides an index (SGHE) of TIE sensitivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a three-compartment model for insulin, coupled with TIESG, is the best model of insulin kinetics for describing glucose homeostasis after a meal.
a three-compartment model, coupled with a glucose-dependent TIE, provides the best description of insulin kinetics and TIE.
the TIE model can be used to estimate insulin sensitivity to glucose, a parameter which is of great interest in the study of the metabolic syndrome and diabetes.
